title: 1  Module 1: Getting Started
text:
1.4 Serial Dilutions

1.4.1 Purpose
Practice accurate small-volume pipetting while learning how serial dilutions work.


1.4.2 Background
You will conduct independent research projects using Delftia acidovorans isolates. For these experiments (and for many future experiments in more advanced laboratory classes and independent research experiences), it is critical that you can pipette small volumes of liquid accurately and precisely. Without this skill, your data will not be reproducible.
Serial dilution is the step-wise dilution of a solution with a known concentration. For example, in the image below, a solution (“Original inoculum”, a concentrated bacterial culture) is being serially diluted 5 times. In the serial dilution shown, each tube is initially filled with 9 ml of “broth” (a liquid medium used for microbial cultures). In this experiment, the “broth” is our diluent – the liquid being used to dilute our solution. Next, 1 ml of the concentrated original inoculum is added to the first tube. The total volume of liquid in this tube is 10 ml (9 ml broth + 1 ml inoculum). Thus, the concentration of the solution in this tube is 1/10 of the concentration in the original inoculum (1 ml original inoculum/10 ml total volume). After the solution in this tube is mixed well, 1 ml is removed and transferred to the next tube. The concentration of the solution in the second tube is now 1/10 of that in the first tube, and 1/100 of that in the original inoculum. For this reason, we would refer to the experiment shown as a 1:10 serial dilution. Note that we use the same dilution factor for every dilution in the series – that is, each time we dilute by a factor of 10, and after five dilutions, the concentration of our last tube is 1/105, or 1/100,000.
Serial dilution is the stepwise dilution of a solution by a constant factor. In this module, you will perform a 1:10 serial dilution of crystal violet in a 96-well plate to connect pipetting technique to the logic of dilution.
Figure Figure 1.2 summarizes the repeated-transfer logic underlying the serial dilution workflow.






Figure 1.2: Serial dilution overview showing stepwise dilution from a concentrated starting sample. Created with BioRender.com.





1.4.3 Protocol
Use Figure Figure 1.3 to plan the first rows of the microplate before starting the transfers.






Figure 1.3: Top rows of a 96-well microplate used to plan the serial dilution setup. Created with BioRender.com.



Today, you will be performing a serial dilution of crystal violet (a purple dye). Instead of tubes, you will perform your dilutions in a 96-well microplate. This is a small, clear plastic plate with 8 rows or 12 small wells. Each well can hold up to ~250 μl of liquid.
For this protocol, your instructor will provide you with the concentrated solution (crystal violet) and the diluent (water).
Before pipetting anything, read the entire protocol (Parts 1-3) and create an experimental plan as described on page 3 (your first lab notebook entry, dated today).

1.4.3.1 Part 1: Lab partner 1 pipettes, lab partner 2 watches.

Pipette 50 μl of water into each well in row A of your microplate.
Carefully raise the plate to eye level and examine the wells from the side. Does it look like you pipetted the same volume into each well?
Pipette 50 μl of crystal violet solution only into well A1.
Using your pipetter, mix the liquids in well A1 by slowly and gently “pipetting up and down”. Be sure to depress the pipette plunger only to the first stop.
After mixing, be sure that you have fully dispensed all of the liquid from your pipette tip.
Eject your pipette tip into your red waste bag.
With a new tip, transfer 50 μl from well A1 into well A2.
Repeat the mixing procedure used for well A1.
After mixing, be sure that you have fully dispensed all of the liquid from your pipette tip.
Eject your pipette tip into your red waste bag.
Repeat this process until you have transferred 50 μl from well A11 into well A12.
After mixing the liquids in well A12, draw 50 μl into your pipette tip as if you were going to continue diluting into well “A13”.
Dispense the 50 μl into your waste container and eject your tip.



1.4.3.2 Part 2: Lab partner 2 pipets; lab partner 1 watches.
Lab partner 2 should repeat the exact same protocol, using Row B of the microplate.


1.4.3.3 Part 3: Repeat!
Lab partner 1 should repeat the exact same protocol, using Row C, and then lab partner 2 should repeat the exact same protocol, using Row D.


1.4.3.4 Part 4: Add a Negative Control.
Add 100 μl of water to well H12.


1.4.3.5 Part 5: Visual observations and data analysis.

Compare Rows A and B. Do you see any differences? Consider the overall pattern of color intensity going from left to right (column 1 to column 12), and also compare each well (i.e., compare well A1 to well B1 and A2 to B2). Answer the relevant question on the post-lab.
Compare Rows C and D. Answer the relevant question on the post-lab.
Compare Row A to Row C (partner 1’s rows) and Row B to Row D (partner 2’s rows). Answer the relevant question on the post-lab.
Ask your instructor to help you use the lab’s microplate reader to measure the absorbance of the solutions in each well of your microplate.
Take a picture of your data.

Before you start actually pipetting, you should have your plan approved by your instructor. Below is an image of the top two rows of a 96-well microplate. Draw a similar image in your lab notebook. Then, using the serial dilution diagram shown on page 1 as a model, draw how you will set up your serial dilutions. (It is not necessary to draw this twice; just show what you will do with Row A.)
To do this correctly, read the protocol and indicate the following in your lab notebook using the diagram as appropriate and/or making a bulleted list beside the diagram. 1) Where does the water go? 2) How much water are you pipetting? 3) Where does the crystal violet dye go? 4) How much of the dye will you pipette first? 5) Then what do you do? 6) What steps do you repeat? 7) What do you do after you mix the crystal violet with the water in well A12?
After you’ve finished drawing your plan, use a pen or pencil to shade the wells in row B to predict the color intensity (darkness or lightness) of the solution in each well.
Answer the following questions in your lab notebook: What is the dilution factor for this serial dilution? *If you don’t remember, read back over the explanation of the serial dilution technique above. Compared to the concentrated crystal violet solution provided by your instructor, how dilute will your final sample (well A12 or B12) be?
After you’ve had your plan checked and completed your dilutions, answer the following questions in your lab notebook: - Does your plate look like you predicted it would? - Compare your results to the shading you drew on page 3. If not, what looks different? - Compare your replicates with your partner’s. Are all four rows similar? If not, what is different?
After you’ve measured your plate with the plate reader, answer the following question in your lab notebook: - Did the numerical (quantitative) data obtained from the plate reader match your visual (qualitative) observations? Why or why not?
You can assess how well you performed your serial dilutions by measuring whether each subsequent well shows a decrease in optical density. Do you have any surprises?

3.5.2 Methods: Liquid Culture Setup

Isolated colonies of your bacteria were picked and transferred to a liquid culture medium.
Inoculated liquid culture tubes were placed in a shaker at 30°C (degrees Celsius) overnight with shaking (200-250 RPM).



3.5.3 Methods: Growth Assay Setup
Figure Figure 3.1 provides a reusable 96-well template for mapping control wells and isolate conditions before loading the plate.






Figure 3.1: Blank 96-well plate layout for planning growth-curve wells and controls.




For growth curves, obtain your overnight cultures and prepare 1:1000 dilutions as follows:


25 µl of overnight culture into 25 ml of fresh TSB prepared for you for your positive control (Delftia acidovorans SPH-1) and your isolate.
25 µl of the overnight TSB control into 25 ml of fresh TSB prepared for you as your negative control


Mix each 50 mL conical tube by inverting several times and vortexing.
Carefully pour your diluted cultures into a white plastic sterile reservoir.

Use one plastic reservoir for the positive control and use a separate one for the negative control
Prepare your plastic reservoir when you are ready to use it to avoid contamination!

With a multichannel set to 100 ul, take 8 p200 tips and pipette 100 µl of culture into columns of a 96-well plate as follows. Keep the plate covered with the lid whenever possible to prevent contamination.

Columns 1 and 12 will receive TSB alone - pipette last to minimize contamination
Column 2 will receive TSB + Delftia acidovorans SPH-1
Columns 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, and 11 will receive your TSB + Delftia isolate.

Seal the plate with a breathable seal and load it into the plate reader.
Incubate at 30°C with shaking and collect OD600 measurements over 48 hours.



3.5.4 Methods: Biofilm Assay Setup
Figure Figure 3.2 shows the 96-well layout used for the Module 3 biofilm assay.






Figure 3.2: Biofilm assay plate layout for assigning controls and isolate wells in a 96-well plate.




Prepare fresh 1:1000 dilutions of the positive control, your isolate, and the negative control in fresh TSB.
Transfer 100 µL of each dilution to the assigned wells in the biofilm plate.
Add the peg lid carefully without contaminating the pegs or splashing between wells.
Incubate the biofilm plate statically at 30°C for 48 hours.



3.5.5 Methods: Biofilm Viability
Figure Figure 3.3 outlines the wash-and-detection workflow used to measure biofilm viability after incubation.






Figure 3.3: Biofilm viability workflow using wash plates and detection reagent.




Wash the peg lid using PBS in separate plates to remove planktonic cells.
Prepare the detection reagent using WST solution, electron mediator reagent, and TSB.
Transfer the washed peg lid to the reagent plate and incubate at 37°C.
Measure absorbance at 450 nm after the incubation period.

Record any mistakes, deviations, contamination concerns, or isolate-specific observations in your ELN.

4.5.2 Methods: Turbidimeter
We will swab bacterial cells from your agar plates (BUG Agar: BUG (Biolog Universal Growth) Agar w/ 5% sheep blood), dilute in Biolog IF-A inoculation fluid, and check turbidity with a turbidimeter.
Each student researcher pair will need:

IF-A inoculating fluid
BUG agar plate with bacteria (incubated overnight at 33°C from your TSA plates)
Biolog GEN3 plate
One 200/300 μl multichannel micropipette (p200)
Micropipette tips for p200
Wipes
Tip disposal container


Calibrate the turbidimeter to a “blank” sample of inoculation fluid in a tube


Using the Biolog Turbidimeter, blank the turbidimeter with a clean tube (wiped clean of dirt and fingerprints) containing uninoculated IF-A. Because the tubes used are not optically uniform, they should be blanked individually.
Set the 100% transmittance adjustment knob so that the meter reads 100%.
Record the reading.


Use a turbidimeter with a bacterial sample in the inoculation fluid in a tube


Collect bacteria from your streak plate by touching the Inoculatorz™ swab to the bacteria (be gentle: do not push the swab through the agar media).
Open your Inoculating Fluid (IF) tube and submerge the swab in the liquid. Swirl the swab around in the fluid for 15 seconds to ensure inoculation. Do not leave the liquid uncapped longer than necessary to prevent contamination. The tubes are glass: work carefully.
Cap the tube and gently invert it three (3) times to ensure thorough mixing (no bubbles).
The target cell density for our protocol is 95%T.







Note



Add more bacteria with the swab, if necessary, to get as close to this value as possible by continuing to add bacteria to the tube. Work carefully and keep the tube capped. If necessary, use another swab if you think it has touched another surface.



Once you’ve reached the target cell density at 95%T, cap the tube and proceed to the next Activity.



4.5.3 Methods: Biolog Plate Preparation
Figure Figure 4.2 shows the multichannel loading pattern used to inoculate each column consistently.






Figure 4.2: Loading a Biolog GEN III plate with a multichannel pipette. Created with BioRender.com.




Pour the cell suspension into the multichannel pipette reservoir.
Load 8 tips onto each gasket of the multichannel pipette and fill the tips by drawing up 100 μl of cell suspension from the reservoir.
Use the multichannel to add 100 μl of diluted bacterial culture to each of the 96 wells of the GEN III MicroPlateTM.


If the tips touch the wells, replace your tips before delivering inoculation fluid to the next column. Work carefully to avoid contamination!
Use the technique practiced in Activity 1.


Eject the pipettor tips if any tip touches the wells of the plate, as this can cause cross-contamination between wells. Reload tips as needed.

6.5.2 Methods: What Was Prepared in Advance

Start an overnight culture of your isolate in Tryptic Soy Broth (TSB, 2.5 mL per tube) by using a sterile loop to obtain one colony from an agar plate and inoculate TSB.
Incubate with shaking at 30°C overnight.
For general bacterial inputs, reconstitute the lysozyme in TE buffer to 10 mg/ml. We recommend preparing enzymes freshly on the day, as enzymatic activity reduces over time once reconstituted.



6.5.3 Methods: Day of the Lab

We will follow the Nanopore-only Microbial Isolate Sequencing Solution (NO-MISS) associated extraction protocols.
Obtain your liquid culture and spin down 1.0 mL of culture.
In a fresh 1.5 mL Eppendorf DNA LoBind tube, centrifuge 1,000 µl at 12,000 x g for 1 minute.
Remove the supernatant and resuspend the pellet in 100 µl TE buffer with 10 µl lysozyme.
Incubate at 37°C for 10 minutes in a thermomixer at 500 RPM. If a thermomixer is unavailable, the reaction can be incubated stationary and agitated by gently flicking for 10 seconds every two minutes.
Combine the following reagents with your sample in the 1.5 mL Eppendorf DNA LoBind tube, and mix by vortexing.




Reagent
Volume




Proteinase K
10 uL


RNase A
3 uL


Total (w/ sample)
113 uL




Vortexing your sample before adding the CTAB buffer allows the enzymes to fully mix with the bacterial cells, as the mixture can become viscous.
Add 200 µl of CTAB buffer and mix by vortexing. Extractions performed using the CTAB buffer improve sequencing health and output compared to using NEB Lysis Buffer from the Monarch Spin gDNA Extraction Kit.


IMPORTANT: The full 30-minute incubation must be completed to ensure the proteinase and RNase activity occurs, regardless of turbidity.


Incubate at 56°C for 30 minutes in a thermomixer at 1,000 RPM.


Note: Depending on the bacterial input, the solution may become fully transparent or may remain hazy.
INFO: The Monarch Spin gDNA Extraction Kit is used for gDNA extraction. The remainder of this method is written following the Genomic DNA Binding and Elution protocol with our recommended alterations.


Preheat the Monarch® gDNA Elution Buffer to 60°C for later use.


IMPORTANT: The ratio of binding buffer to lysate (2:1) is important for the column binding efficiency. We recommend taking through 200 µl of lysate for use with 400 µl of binding buffer per sample. To run more samples from the same isolate, the volumes can be increased in relation to the 2:1 ratio of buffer to lysate.


Combine the following reagents in a clean 1.5 mL Eppendorf DNA LoBind tube:




Reagent
Volume




Lysate from the previous step
200 uL


Monarch® gDNA Binding Buffer
400 uL


Total (w/ sample)
600 uL




Ensure the reaction is thoroughly mixed by pipetting until the liquid is homogeneous. Thorough mixing is essential to ensure the DNA binds properly to the column and to homogenise the CTAB and Monarch® gDNA Binding Buffer, which solidify on initial contact.
Transfer the reaction to a Monarch® Spin Column pre-inserted into a Monarch® collection tube, without touching the upper column area.

Close the tube and centrifuge for 3 minutes at 1,000 x g to bind the gDNA and then for 1 minute at maximum speed (>12,000 x g) to clear the membrane. Do not empty or remove the collection tube from the centrifuge when changing settings.
Remove the gDNA spin column from the collection tube and discard the tube with the flow-through.
Transfer the gDNA spin column to a new collection tube and add 500 µl Monarch® gDNA Wash Buffer.

IMPORTANT: Do NOT vortex.

Close the collection tube and invert multiple times until the wash buffer reaches the cap.
Immediately centrifuge the collection tube for 1 minute at maximum speed (>12,000 x g). Remove the gDNA spin column from the collection tube to discard the flow-through.
Re-insert the gDNA spin column into the collection tube, add 500 µl gDNA wash buffer, and close the tube.
Immediately centrifuge the collection tube for 1 minute at maximum speed (>12,000 x g). Remove the gDNA spin column from the collection tube to discard the flow-through.
After centrifugation, ensure there is no liquid in the gDNA spin column above or below the silica membrane. If there is liquid, repeat the centrifugation until all liquid is removed.

IMPORTANT: Preheating the Monarch® gDNA Elution Buffer to 60°C is essential for maximum recovery of larger gDNA fragments.

Place the gDNA spin column in a DNase-free 1.5 mL microfuge tube and add 100 µl of preheated Monarch® gDNA Elution Buffer. Close the tube and incubate at room temperature for 1 minute.

TIP: If extractions are not yielding high enough concentrations of DNA for 200 ng per sample, less gDNA elution buffer can be run through the column to increase the concentration.
Note: Elution of less than 100 µl results in lower total yield, and elution of less than 50 µl is not recommended.
We recommend repeating the elution by passing 100 µl of eluate through the column once more.

Centrifuge for 1 minute at maximum speed (>12,000 x g) to elute the gDNA into the 1.5 mL microfuge tube. The gDNA spin column can be discarded.
Quantify 1 µl of eluted sample using a Qubit fluorometer.

Add 1 µl of eluted sample (DNA) to a Qubit tube with 199 µl of 1X High Sensitivity (HS) Assay mix.
Record the DNA concentration in your notes and on the tubes.
The expected yield is ~15-20 ng/µl per sample with a DNA Integrity Number (DIN) of 9.
Store at 4 or 20°C until use.

8.5 Procedures

8.5.1 Lab Safety

8.5.1.1 Before Lab

Wear the correct PPE (lab coat, goggles, and gloves).
Wipe the lab bench with 70% ethanol.
Before working with microorganisms, carefully wipe pipettors with 70% ethanol.



8.5.1.2 During Lab

Treat all tips as potential biohazards.
Remove your PPE if you are leaving the lab (water/bio break).
Discard samples and disposable lab items in the correct trash bins.
Try to keep personal items (computers, phones, etc.) usage to a minimum.



8.5.1.3 After Lab

Wipe your station with 70% alcohol.
If you touched any personal items during the lab, wipe them with 70% ethanol before leaving.
Dispose of gloves in the main biohazard waste container.
Dispose of used petri dishes in the biohazard bin.
All liquids containing bacteria must be poured into a beaker for bleach decontamination (can be found on the blue bench paper by this sink labeled “liquid”).
Glass tubes can be placed into a beaker (on the blue bench paper by this sink, labeled “glass”).
All bacterial growth plates can be thrown away in the biohazard trash.
Return all reusable materials to our storage drawers.
Wipe down all surfaces with ethanol.
Remove PPE.
Wash your hands.
